passages.t: Unwashed hands and a gift to God
passages.happening: Religious leaders come up from Jerusalem to look Jesus over. They notice that some of his disciples eat without first washing their hands in the proper religious way. They ask him why his followers do not keep the tradition of the elders. Jesus answers with hard words. He quotes the prophet Isaiah about people who honour God with their lips while their hearts are far away. Then he gives an example. A man could call his money a gift set apart for God, and in that way get out of caring for his own father and mother. Jesus says that this kind of rule cancels the word of God.
passages.hearers:
Mark stops to explain the washing, because many of his first readers were not Jews. This was not about germs. It was about being ritually clean, which means fit to come near God. The law of Moses told the priests to wash their hands and feet before they served at the altar (Exodus 30:19-21). The Pharisees, a group devoted to keeping the law with great care, wanted ordinary people at ordinary meals to live with the same holiness as priests. So they washed before eating, and they washed cups and pots too.

These extra rules were called the tradition of the elders. They were taught by word of mouth and later written down in the Mishnah, a book of Jewish law put together around AD 200. The Mishnah records two schools of teachers from before Jesus' time arguing about whether to wash hands before or after pouring the cup at a meal (Mishnah Berakhot 8:2). So handwashing was already a living question in Jesus' day.

The word Corban is Hebrew. It means an offering, something brought near to God. A man could declare his goods Corban, devoted to God, and then his parents could not touch them. Burial boxes for bones from around Jerusalem in this period have been found with the word carved on them, used as a kind of 'hands off' label. Taking vows seriously was right: the law says that a man who makes a vow “must not break his word” (Numbers 30:2). But this vow was being used as a door out of a plain duty. Later Jewish teachers agreed with Jesus here. The Mishnah allows such a vow to be undone when it concerns a man and his own parents (Mishnah Nedarim 9:1).
passages.ot: Jesus quotes Isaiah 29:13. In the Berean Standard Bible, Isaiah reads: “These people draw near to Me with their mouths and honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me.” Then he quotes two commands from Moses: honour your father and mother (Exodus 20:12), and the death penalty for cursing them (Exodus 21:17). For Jesus the written command of God stands above every human rule, however holy it looks.
passages.hard: Is Jesus against all tradition? No. The word tradition simply means something handed on, and Paul uses the same word for the teaching he passed on to the churches (2 Thessalonians 2:15). Christians still argue about how much weight church tradition should carry. Some give it great authority alongside Scripture. Others hold that Scripture alone is the final judge of every tradition. What Jesus condemns here is narrower and clear to all sides: any rule that lets a person dodge what God plainly commands.
passages.asks: The Corban trick looked like devotion and worked as an escape. Ask whether any of your religious habits do the same: busy church work that excuses neglect at home, or giving that makes you feel free of harder duties. Ask who in your family is owed care that you have quietly set aside.

passages.t: What really makes a person unclean
passages.happening: Jesus calls the crowd back and gives them a short saying, almost a riddle: nothing that goes into a person from outside can make him unclean, but what comes out of him can. Later, in the house, the disciples ask what he meant. He says that food goes into the stomach, not the heart, and then passes out of the body. Mark adds his own short comment: “Thus all foods are clean.” Then Jesus names what does come from the heart: evil thoughts, sexual sin, theft, murder, greed, lies, envy, pride, and more.
passages.hearers:
This would have been startling. The law of Moses had a long list of clean and unclean foods (Leviticus 11). Pork, for example, was forbidden. Keeping those laws was one of the clearest marks of being a Jew. Jesus moves the whole question from the plate to the heart.

In the Bible, the heart is not mainly the place of feelings. It is the centre of the person, where thinking, choosing, and wanting all begin. So when Jesus says evil comes 'from within', he means it starts in who we are, not just in what we touch.

Mark's comment, 'all foods are clean', may have meant a great deal to his first readers. The early church argued hard about whether non-Jewish believers had to keep the food laws, and whether Jewish believers could eat with them. Peter heard a voice in a vision say, “Do not call anything impure that God has made clean” (Acts 10:15).
passages.ot: The prophets had already said that the real problem lies in the heart. “The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure” (Jeremiah 17:9). David prayed, “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Psalm 51:10). And God promised through Ezekiel, “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26). No washing of hands can reach that deep. Only God can.
passages.hard: Did Jesus himself cancel the food laws, or did the church draw that conclusion later? Scholars differ. The Greek of verse 19 most naturally means that Jesus, by saying this, was making all foods clean, and most modern Bibles read it that way. Some scholars, including some Jewish scholars, argue that Jesus was only setting aside the newer handwashing rules, not the laws of Moses on food, and that the wider conclusion came later. Many others hold that Mark's comment states plainly what Jesus' words meant. Either way, by the time Mark wrote, the church understood that Christians were free to eat all foods (Acts 10; Romans 14:14).
passages.asks: It is easier to worry about what is out there, the wrong films, the wrong people, the wrong places, than to look at what is in here. Read Jesus' list slowly. Ask which of these things grows in your own heart, and what it would mean to bring that to God instead of only guarding the doors.

passages.happening: Jesus goes north into the region of Tyre, outside Jewish land, and tries to stay hidden in a house. A Greek woman, born in that part of Syria, hears about him. Her little daughter is held by an unclean spirit. She falls at his feet and keeps begging him to help. Jesus answers, “First let the children have their fill,” and then, “For it is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the dogs.” She replies at once, “Yes, Lord,” and then, “even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.” Jesus tells her that because of this answer the demon has left her daughter. She goes home and finds the girl well.
passages.hearers:
Tyre was an old port city on the coast, rich from trade. Its silver coins were so pure that they were the coins used to pay the yearly tax to the temple in Jerusalem. Tyre and its neighbour Sidon bought food from the farmland around Galilee: the Bible says “their region depended on the king’s country for food” (Acts 12:20). So Jews and the people of Tyre lived close together, and not always as friends.

The woman is a Gentile, someone who is not a Jew. Matthew calls her “a Canaanite woman” (Matthew 15:22), the old name for Israel's enemies in the land. In the Bible, dogs were mostly wild animals of the street, and 'dog' could be an insult. A Jewish hearer would understand Jesus' picture at once. The children are Israel, whom God called his son (Exodus 4:22). The bread is what God gives his people.

The word Jesus uses means a little dog, a house dog. The woman grabs hold of that. House dogs are inside, under the table, and they eat from the same meal. She is not asking for the children's place. She is asking for a crumb, and she believes a crumb from him is enough.
passages.ot: God told Abraham that “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3). Israel was chosen first, but never only for itself. Paul later describes the same order Jesus names here: the good news is “first to the Jew, then to the Greek” (Romans 1:16).
passages.hard: Jesus' words sound harsh, even insulting. Readers have taken them in more than one way. Some think Jesus was testing her faith, the way a teacher sets a hard question to draw out a good answer. Some think the saying was a real statement of his mission, which was first to Israel (Matthew 15:24), and that her answer showed how that mission would reach beyond Israel. Some read it as a moment when Jesus is moved by her reply. What is clear is that he does not send her away. The word 'first' already leaves a door open, and he grants her request in full. She is the only person in Mark who argues with Jesus and wins, and the only one who calls him 'Lord'.
passages.asks: She took the hard word without giving up and without getting offended. She did not demand. She trusted. Ask how you pray when God seems slow or silent. Do you walk away, or do you keep coming, holding on to what you know of his goodness?

passages.happening: Jesus takes a long way round, north to Sidon and then back to the Sea of Galilee, into the Decapolis, a group of Greek cities. People bring him a man who is deaf and can hardly speak. Jesus takes him aside from the crowd. He puts his fingers in the man's ears, spits, and touches his tongue. Then he looks up to heaven, sighs deeply, and says one word in Aramaic, his own everyday language: “Ephphatha!”, which means “Be opened!” At once the man can hear and speak plainly. Jesus tells them to tell no one, but the more he says it, the more they spread the news.
passages.hearers:
The Decapolis was Gentile country, with Greek cities and pagan temples. It was where the man freed from many demons had gone to tell what Jesus had done for him (5:20). Perhaps that is why people there now bring their friend to Jesus.

In the ancient world, many people thought saliva had healing power. The Roman historian Tacitus tells how a blind man in Alexandria begged the emperor Vespasian, around AD 69, to wet his eyes with his spittle. So Jesus' actions would not have looked strange. But Mark makes clear that the healing comes from Jesus' look to heaven and his word, not from a method.

Think of how a deaf man would feel. He could not hear what Jesus said. So Jesus speaks to him by touch: here are your ears, here is your tongue, and up there is where help comes from. He takes him away from the crowd so the man is not a show.
passages.ot: Isaiah promised a day when God would come to save his people: “Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped” (Isaiah 35:5). The next verse says “the mute tongue will shout for joy” (Isaiah 35:6). Mark's Greek word for a man who can 'hardly speak' is very rare. It appears nowhere else in the New Testament, and in the Greek Old Testament only in that very verse of Isaiah. Mark is telling his readers: the promise of Isaiah 35 is coming true. And Isaiah 35 begins, “Behold, your God will come.”
passages.hard:
Why does Jesus sigh? The word means to groan. It is the same word Paul uses for how we “groan inwardly” as we wait for God to make all things new (Romans 8:23). Jesus is not tired or annoyed. He feels the weight of a broken world, where ears do not hear and tongues are bound. The healing does not come from a distance. It comes from someone who feels the pain of it.

The church remembered this moment for a long time. In Milan in the late 300s, the bishop Ambrose explained to new Christians that before their baptism their ears had been touched and the word Ephphatha spoken, so that their ears would be opened to God's word.
passages.asks: The crowd says, “He has done all things well!” Just after this, Jesus will ask his own disciples whether they have ears and still do not hear (8:18). The deaf man is a picture of them, and of us. Ask where you have stopped hearing God, and ask him to say 'Be opened' to you.
